title: Serving runtime profiling tooling and scripts - runbook v3
content:
Purpose:
This runbook collects the recommended tooling, scripts, and CI patterns we use to investigate performance regressions and bottlenecks in the serving runtime. It focuses on practical, repeatable steps to capture CPU/GPU flamegraphs, traces, and CI-based perf checks so engineers can triage latency regressions and identify hotspots quickly.

When to use this doc:
- Sudden increase in P50/P95 serving latency
- Regression after a model or runtime change
- Unexplained throughput drop or increased tail latency
- High CPU/GPU utilization without clear culprit

Prereqs / credentials / access:
- SSH access to test node(s) or reproducer environment (staging/dedicated test pool)
- sudo or perf capabilities (CAP_SYS_ADMIN or perf_event_paranoid appropriately set)
- NVidia drivers + Nsight/NSYS installed for GPU profiling (if applicable)
- FlameGraph utilities installed (stackcollapse-perf.pl, flamegraph.pl) on analysis host
- Access to tracing backend (Jaeger/Zipkin) and log aggregation (Stackdriver/Datadog)

Core tools we use (short list):
- perf (kernel CPU sampling), FlameGraph (Brendan Gregg scripts)
- bpftrace / eBPF tooling for kernel-level tracing heatmaps
- nsight systems (nsys) and nvprof for CUDA kernel traces (prefer nsys)
- py-spy / scylla-profile for python-level sampling (safe to use in prod)
- pprof (gperftools/pprof) or jemalloc/heaptrack for memory profiling
- jaeger/zipkin for distributed traces, grpc interceptors for spans

Quick triage checklist:
1) Confirm reproducibility (load/traffic pattern) and capture simple metrics (top, iostat, nvidia-smi).
2) Determine if CPU-bound or GPU-bound. If GPU utilization high, start with nsys.
3) If CPU-bound, reproduce request and start perf sampling on target process.
4) Generate flamegraph(s) and annotate with route/model/commit.
5) Correlate with logs and distributed traces.
6) Open an incident PR with captured artifacts (flame.svg, perf.data, trace.json).

Collecting a CPU flamegraph (Linux):
(Use a staging node with the failing workload or replay traffic on a bench instance)
- Identify PID(s) of serving process: ps aux | grep redwood-serving
- Run perf sampling for 20s (adjust time for steady-state):
  sudo perf record -F 99 -p <PID> -g -- sleep 20
- Convert to script output and collapse stacks:
  sudo perf script > perf.unfolded
  ./stackcollapse-perf.pl perf.unfolded > perf.folded
- Generate flamegraph:
  ./flamegraph.pl --title "serving-runtime CPU flamegraph - <route> - <commit>" perf.folded > flame.svg
- Upload flame.svg to the incident ticket and include perf.data for deeper analysis.
Notes:
- Use -F between 99-499 depending on load and overhead tolerance. Higher sample freq gives finer detail but more overhead.
- If perf record fails with permission errors, set /proc/sys/kernel/perf_event_paranoid to 1 or 0 (temporarily) or use sudo.

Collecting Python-level stacks (py-spy):
- Install py-spy on analysis host.
- sudo py-spy record -o pyspy.svg --pid <PID> --duration 20 --native
- py-spy is safe to run on production (non-intrusive) and produces a flamegraph svg. Use --python to limit to python frames.

GPU profiling with Nsight Systems (nsys) - focus on CUDA kernels and NVTX spans:
- Basic profile for 30s:
  nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt --sample=cpu --duration=30 -o nsys_report ./start-serving.sh
- Export report to HTML for inspection: nsys-ui nsys_report.qdrep
- For kernel-level throughput detail use Nsight Compute (ncu) for single-kernel runs.
Notes:
- Ensure nvtx annotations exist in the runtime (we annotate batch boundaries and model load/hotpath via nvtx ranges).
- GPU profiling adds overhead; prefer staging/dedicated reproducer.

Distributed traces / request-level sampling:
- Increase sampler or use on-demand trace for slow requests. For gRPC HTTP routes we recommend attaching a unique request-id and sampling spans to Jaeger.
- Use the console to search by request-id, then correlate service spans with CPU/GPU hotspots.

Perf CI jobs (recommended patterns):
- Purpose: catch regressions in critical hotspots and tail latency across PRs/commits.
- Two-tier approach: quick smoke on PR (low-cost, synthetic short-run) + nightly full-run (longer, aggregated).

Example GitHub Actions job (simplified):
name: perf-pr-check
permissions: read-all
on: [pull_request]
jobs:
  perf-smoke:
    runs-on: [self-hosted, perf-runner]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      - name: Build benchmark image
        run: ./build/perf-image.sh
      - name: Run synthetic load (20s)
        run: |
          docker run --rm -e MODEL=test-model perf-image ./bench --qps 100 --duration 20 --route /generate 
      - name: Capture CPU stacks
        run: |
          PID=$(pgrep -f "redwood-serving") && sudo perf record -F 200 -p $PID -g -- sleep 20 && sudo perf script > perf.unfolded
      - name: Generate small flamegraph
        run: ./stackcollapse-perf.pl perf.unfolded | ./flamegraph.pl --width 1200 > perf-pr-flame.svg
      - name: Upload artifact
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v3
        with:
          name: perf-pr-flame
          path: perf-pr-flame.svg
Notes on CI runners:
- Use self-hosted runners with identical CPU/GPU families to our production fleet to avoid noisy comparisons. Document runner AMI and kernel versions.
- Store baseline artifacts in a checked-in folder or S3 with metadata (commit, kernel, distro, CPU model).

Golden baseline and regression detection:
- We keep a baseline archive for each supported CPU/GPU SKU with: flame.svg, perf.data, sample load profile, and environment metadata.
- Nightly job compares current PR artifact against baseline using heuristics: total stack width on top N frames, P95 of per-request CPU time, and % of time in critical functions (KV cache, attention forward, attention kernel).
- If delta > threshold, the job creates an autopruned analysis issue with attached artifacts.

Collecting kernel-level events / eBPF (when syscalls or scheduler issues suspected):
- Use bpftrace scripts from tools/prof to capture syscall heatmaps, context-switch rates, IRQ/softirq hotspots. Example one-liner:
  sudo bpftrace -e 'tracepoint:sched:sched_switch { @switches[comm] = count(); }' -o sched.txt -d 10
- We also have a repo of bpftrace scripts: tools/prof/bpf/*.bt.

Aggregating traces across replicated pods/nodes:
- To find cross-node skew, sample several pods during the same time window and merge profiles with timestamps. Tag flamegraphs by pod and route.
- For distributed tracing, ensure request-id is propagated and use jaeger to identify the slowest service span chain.

Interpreting flamegraphs (quick guide):
- Wide blocks at top = functions consuming the most samples (hot). Drill down by clicking in the SVG.
- Tall narrow stacks = deep call chains; check if expensive work is being done inline (e.g., serde, tensor copy).
- Flamegraph taxonomies we track: input parsing, model forward (kernel boundary), kv-cache, batching logic, grpc/HTTP overhead. If majority is in model kernel, focus on GPU/quantization.

Common pitfalls and notes:
- Sampling vs instrumentation: sampling preserves timing characteristics; instrumentation can perturb latency. Prefer sampling for tail-latency investigations.
- JIT / symbolization: ensure build includes debug symbols or symbol server configured; use addr2line or py-spy for Python frames.
- Noise from background processes: isolate bench node or pin CPUs/cores to reduce noise.
- Kernel version differences change perf results; always record kernel version in artifact metadata.

Example incident (summary):
- Symptom: sudden P95 increase after a merge.
- Action: ran perf for 30s and generated flamegraph. Found 45% of samples attributed to function serve::batcher::flush().
- Root cause: new batching logic introduced an O(n^2) reallocation when batch size > 64.
- Fix: replaced with pre-reserve vector and added unit test; re-ran perf and P95 returned to baseline.

On-call / escalation steps:
- If perf artifacts show service-level saturation (CPU pinned across cores) but no single hot function: escalate to SRE and infra to check kernel/IO/cgroup settings and noisy neighbor issues.
- If GPU kernels are causing latency spikes and Nsight shows serialization on PCIe transfers: escalate to hw team and consider pinning CPU->GPU NUMA settings.

Useful commands snippet (cheat sheet):
- perf top -p <PID>
- sudo perf record -F 199 -p <PID> -g -- sleep 20
- sudo perf script | ./stackcollapse-perf.pl > perf.folded && ./flamegraph.pl perf.folded > flame.svg
- py-spy record -o pyspy.svg --pid <PID> --duration 20 --native
- nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx --duration=30 -o out ./start-serving.sh
- nsys-ui out.qdrep (open on workstation)

Artifact naming conventions (recommended):
- <team>-<route>-<commit>-<sku>-<date>-<type>
  e.g. serving-bench-generate-9f2ac01-c5.6xlarge-20260301-cpu-flame.svg

Storage and retention:
- Upload raw perf.data, pyspy.svg, nsys.qdrep, and a rendered SVG to S3 under s3://redwood-perf/artifacts/<year>/<month>/<commit>/
- Keep nightly baselines for 90 days, PR-level artifacts for 30 days (configurable).

References and further reading:
- FlameGraph repo: https://github.com/brendangregg/FlameGraph
- Brendan Gregg's perf tutorial and flamegraph writing
- NVIDIA Nsight Systems docs for GPU tracing
- internal: tools/prof/README.md (scripts and bpftrace examples)

Contact / owners:
- Primary owner: Aisha Patel (eng-serving-runtime)
- Secondary: Liam O'Connor; on-call SRE when investigating infra-related noise

Appendix: small helper scripts (where they live)
- tools/prof/generate-flame.sh  - wrapper around perf + stackcollapse + flamegraph.pl
- tools/prof/ci-perf-runner/  - self-hosted GitHub Actions runner images and setup docs
- tools/prof/bpf/  - collection of bpftrace scripts for common investigations

TL;DR: Start with reproducible load, determine CPU vs GPU, collect a sampled flamegraph (perf/py-spy/nsys), compare to baseline, and attach artifacts to the ticket. Use the provided CI patterns to catch regressions earlier.
